tool.name: Git
tool.tagline: Distributed version control for tracking and sharing code changes
tool.description: Git records the history of a project as a series of snapshots and lets many people work on it in parallel through branches, merges and remotes. It is the version control system behind GitHub, GitLab and nearly every software team, so fluency in it is a baseline skill for any developer.

concepts.name: What version control is
concepts.summary: Version control records every change to a set of files so you can compare, undo and share work safely.
concepts.why: Every software team uses it; without it, collaboration and recovering from mistakes are guesswork.
concepts.body:
A **version control system** (VCS) keeps the full history of a project: who changed what, when, and why. Instead of `report-final-v3-REALLY-final.docx`, you have one set of files plus a timeline of snapshots you can return to at any moment.

Older systems such as Subversion are **centralized**: one server holds the history and everyone checks files out from it. Git is **distributed**: every clone is a complete copy of the repository, history included. That means you can commit, browse history, branch and diff while offline, and any clone can serve as a backup.

Git thinks in **snapshots**, not lists of edits. Each commit records what the whole project looked like at that moment, plus a message and a pointer to the commit(s) before it. Unchanged files are stored once and shared between snapshots, so this is cheap.

What you get from it in daily work:

- A safety net: any committed state can be recovered, so experimenting is cheap.
- Collaboration: several people change the same project in parallel and Git combines their work.
- Answers to "why is this line here?" through commit messages and blame.
- Branches: isolated lines of work that can be merged back later.

Git is the de facto standard, and hosting services such as GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket add code review, CI and issue tracking on top of it. Git itself is just the command-line tool and file format; it works fine with no server at all.
takeaways: Git stores snapshots of the whole project, linked into a history
Distributed: every clone has the full history and works offline
Git is the tool; GitHub/GitLab are hosting services built around it
pitfalls: Thinking Git and GitHub are the same thing — Git runs locally without any account or server.

quiz.q: What does 'distributed' mean for Git?
options: Files are split across several servers
Every clone contains the complete history
Each developer may only edit their own files
Commits are sent to the server immediately
quiz.explain: A Git clone is a full repository, so history, commits and branches all work locally.

quiz.q: How does Git primarily think about a commit?
options: As a snapshot of the whole project plus metadata
As a list of line edits to one file
As a zip file uploaded to a server
As a copy of only the files you opened
quiz.explain: Each commit records the full project state; unchanged files are shared, not duplicated.

concepts.name: Install and configure Git
concepts.summary: Install Git, set your name and email, and pick sane defaults with git config.
concepts.why: Every commit is stamped with your identity, and a few defaults save pain later.
concepts.body:
Install Git from your package manager (`apt install git`, `brew install git`, `winget install Git.Git`) or from git-scm.com, then check it with `git --version`.

Before your first commit, tell Git who you are. Name and email are written into every commit you make, so use the email your hosting account knows about:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
```

`git config` works at three **levels**, each overriding the one before:

- `--system`: every user on the machine.
- `--global`: you, stored in `~/.gitconfig`.
- `--local` (the default inside a repo): one repository, stored in `.git/config`.

So you can keep a personal email globally and override it with a work email inside work repositories. `git config --list --show-origin` shows every value and which file it came from, which is the quickest way to debug a surprising setting.

A few settings worth setting on day one:

- `init.defaultBranch main` so new repositories start on `main`.
- `core.editor` to an editor you can use (`"code --wait"`, `nano`, `vim`), because Git opens it for commit messages.
- `pull.rebase false` (or `true`) so `git pull` knows how to combine diverged histories instead of asking every time.

On Windows, `core.autocrlf true` converts line endings for you; on macOS/Linux leave it unset or `input`.
concepts.code:
git --version                         # git version 2.51.0
git config --global user.name "Ada Lovelace"
git config --global user.email "ada@example.com"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git config --global pull.rebase false

git config user.email                 # read one value
git config --list --show-origin       # every setting and its file
takeaways: Set user.name and user.email before your first commit
Config levels: system < global (~/.gitconfig) < local (.git/config)
git config --list --show-origin explains where a value comes from
pitfalls: Committing with a wrong email — the commits won't be linked to your hosting account and fixing them later means rewriting history.

quiz.q: You set user.email globally, then a different user.email with --local inside repo A. Which email do commits in repo A use?
quiz.explain: Local config overrides global, which overrides system.

concepts.name: Create or clone a repository
concepts.summary: Start tracking a project with git init, or copy an existing repository with git clone.
concepts.why: Every Git workflow starts with a repository; these two commands are how you get one.
concepts.body:
A **repository** is a project folder plus a hidden `.git` directory. That `.git` directory *is* the repository: it holds every commit, branch and setting. The files you see around it are just the currently checked-out version.

There are two ways to get one.

**`git init`** turns the current folder into a new, empty repository. Nothing is tracked yet; you choose what to add and commit. Use it for brand-new projects or to start versioning an existing folder.

**`git clone <url>`** copies an existing repository, usually from a server. It downloads the full history, checks out the default branch into a new folder and remembers the source as a remote named `origin`. URLs come in two common flavours:

- HTTPS, `https://github.com/user/repo.git`, which authenticates with a token or credential helper.
- SSH, `git@github.com:user/repo.git`, which authenticates with your SSH key.

You can pass a folder name as a second argument (`git clone <url> myapp`).

Because the repository lives in `.git`, deleting that folder deletes all history and leaves plain files behind. Moving or renaming the project folder is fine; Git doesn't care where it lives.

Don't create a repository inside another one by accident (for example running `git init` in your home directory). Run `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` if you are unsure which repository you are in.
concepts.code:
# Brand-new project
mkdir notes && cd notes
git init                      # Initialized empty Git repository in .../notes/.git/
ls -a                         # .  ..  .git

# Copy an existing project with its full history
git clone https://github.com/git/git.git
git clone git@github.com:me/app.git my-app   # SSH, into folder my-app
cd my-app
git remote -v                 # origin  git@github.com:me/app.git (fetch/push)
takeaways: The .git directory is the repository; the rest is a working copy
git init starts empty; git clone copies full history and sets up origin
HTTPS uses tokens, SSH uses keys
pitfalls: Running git init in your home folder, which makes every file under it look untracked.

quiz.q: What does git clone give you besides the files?
options: Nothing else; history stays on the server
The full history and a remote named origin
quiz.explain: Clone copies the whole repository and records where it came from as origin.

concepts.name: Working tree, index and repository
concepts.summary: Git moves changes through three places: the working tree you edit, the staging index, and the committed history.
concepts.why: Almost every Git command is about moving changes between these areas, so this model makes the rest click.
concepts.body:
Git keeps your project in three places at once, and understanding them explains most commands.

- The **working tree** is the files on disk that you edit with your editor.
- The **index** (also called the **staging area**) is a draft of the next commit. It starts as a copy of the last commit, and you update it explicitly.
- The **repository** (`.git`) holds the committed snapshots. `HEAD` points at the commit you currently have checked out.

The normal flow is: edit files in the working tree, `git add` to copy the changes you want into the index, then `git commit` to turn the index into a new permanent snapshot.

Why have a middle step? Because it lets you **shape commits**. You may have touched five files while fixing a bug and tidying up; you can stage just the bug fix, commit it with a clear message, then stage and commit the tidy-up separately. `git add -p` even lets you stage individual hunks within a file.

This model also explains the two kinds of diff. `git diff` compares working tree against the index (what you have *not* staged yet), while `git diff --staged` compares the index against `HEAD` (what *will* go into the next commit).

Files also have a tracking state: **untracked** (Git has never been told about them), **tracked and unmodified**, **modified**, or **staged**. `git status` reports exactly these states.
concepts.code:
echo "hello" > a.txt
git status --short        # ?? a.txt   (untracked)
git add a.txt
git status --short        # A  a.txt   (staged)
git commit -m "Add a.txt"
echo "world" >> a.txt
git status --short        #  M a.txt   (modified, not staged)
git diff                  # working tree vs index
git add a.txt
git diff --staged         # index vs HEAD: what the next commit contains
takeaways: Working tree -> git add -> index -> git commit -> repository
The index is the draft of your next commit
git diff = unstaged changes; git diff --staged = what you are about to commit
pitfalls: Editing a file again after git add and committing — only the staged version is committed, not the later edit.

quiz.q: You edit app.py, run git add app.py, then edit app.py again and commit. What is committed?
options: The version as it was when you ran git add
Nothing, because the file changed after staging
quiz.explain: Commit records the index, which holds the content from the moment you staged it.

quiz.q: Which command shows what the next commit will contain?
quiz.explain: --staged compares the index with HEAD, i.e. exactly what commit would record.

concepts.name: Staging and committing
concepts.summary: Use git add to stage changes and git commit to record them with a clear message.
concepts.why: Commits are the unit of history; good ones make review, debugging and reverting easy.
concepts.body:
`git add <path>` stages the current content of files: new files, modifications and (with `git add -A` or `git add .`) deletions. `git commit` then records the staged snapshot with a message.

Useful forms:

- `git add file.py dir/`: stage specific paths.
- `git add -p`: walk through each change hunk and choose `y`/`n`. The best way to split unrelated changes into separate commits.
- `git commit -m "message"`: commit with a one-line message; without `-m` Git opens your editor.
- `git commit -a`: stage all modifications to *tracked* files and commit in one go. It skips new files.
- `git commit --amend`: replace the last commit with a new one that includes what is staged now, or just fix its message. Only do this before pushing.

A good commit is **one logical change** that leaves the project working. Write the message for a future reader: a short summary line (about 50 characters, imperative mood: "Fix rounding in invoice totals"), a blank line, then a body explaining *why* if it isn't obvious.

Each commit gets an ID, a hash such as `3f9a2c1...`, derived from its content and its parent. You can refer to it by the first 7 or so characters. Change anything about a commit, even its message, and you get a new ID; this is why amending pushed commits causes trouble for others.

Commit early and often locally. Small commits are cheap and easier to review, revert and bisect than one giant "WIP" commit.
concepts.code:
git add src/invoice.py              # stage one file
git add -p                          # pick hunks interactively
git commit -m "Fix rounding in invoice totals"

# Longer message: summary, blank line, body
git commit -m "Cache exchange rates" -m "Rates were fetched per line item, making large invoices slow."

# Forgot a file? Add it to the last (unpushed) commit
git add tests/test_invoice.py
git commit --amend --no-edit

git log --oneline -3
# 9c1e2ab Cache exchange rates
# 3f9a2c1 Fix rounding in invoice totals
takeaways: git add stages; git commit records the staged snapshot
git add -p lets you split unrelated edits into separate commits
One logical change per commit, imperative summary line
--amend rewrites the last commit; don't amend what you've pushed
pitfalls: Expecting git commit -a to include brand-new files — it only stages files Git already tracks.

quiz.q: You created new.py and modified old.py. What does git commit -a -m 'x' commit?
quiz.explain: -a auto-stages modifications to tracked files only; untracked new.py is left out.

quiz.q: Why does git commit --amend change the commit's ID?
options: The ID is a hash of the commit's contents and metadata
Amend also deletes the parent commit
It doesn't; the ID stays the same
quiz.explain: The hash covers the snapshot, message, author and parent, so any change yields a new ID.

concepts.name: Inspecting changes: status and diff
concepts.summary: Read git status and git diff to know exactly what changed before you commit.
concepts.why: Checking status and diff before every commit is the habit that prevents most accidental commits.
concepts.body:
`git status` is the command you will run most. It tells you the current branch, how it compares to its upstream (ahead/behind), and lists files in three groups: staged, not staged, and untracked. It also prints hints for the obvious next commands. `git status -s` gives a compact two-column view: the left column is the index, the right column is the working tree (`M` modified, `A` added, `D` deleted, `??` untracked).

`git diff` shows line-level changes in **unified diff** format. Lines starting with `-` were removed, `+` were added, and `@@ -12,7 +12,8 @@` headers say where each hunk sits.

The variants differ only in *which two snapshots* they compare:

- `git diff`: working tree vs index (unstaged changes).
- `git diff --staged` (alias `--cached`): index vs `HEAD` (staged changes).
- `git diff HEAD`: working tree vs last commit (everything).
- `git diff main feature`: tip of one branch vs another.
- `git diff main...feature`: what `feature` changed since it branched off `main`.

Handy flags: `--stat` for a per-file summary, `--name-only` for just paths, `--word-diff` for prose, and `-- path` to limit output to some files.

Get into the habit of `git status` then `git diff --staged` before each commit. It catches debug prints, stray files and secrets before they enter history, where they are much harder to remove.
concepts.code:
git status
# On branch main
# Your branch is ahead of 'origin/main' by 1 commit.
# Changes to be committed:   modified: app.py
# Changes not staged:        modified: README.md
# Untracked files:           notes.txt

git status -s
# M  app.py        <- staged
#  M README.md     <- modified, not staged
# ?? notes.txt

git diff --staged --stat     # app.py | 4 ++--
git diff main...feature -- src/
takeaways: git status: branch, ahead/behind, staged / unstaged / untracked
diff variants differ in which two snapshots they compare
A...B shows what B changed since it diverged from A
pitfalls: Running plain git diff after staging everything, seeing no output, and assuming there are no changes.

quiz.q: You staged all your edits. Which command still shows them?
quiz.explain: Once staged, changes are in the index, so you compare index to HEAD with --staged.

quiz.q: In git status -s output ' M file.txt' (space, then M), what does it mean?
options: Modified in the working tree but not staged
quiz.explain: The left column is the index, the right column the working tree; M on the right means unstaged.

concepts.name: Reading history with git log
concepts.summary: Browse, filter and search commit history with git log, git show and git blame.
concepts.why: Understanding why code is the way it is starts with reading its history.
concepts.body:
`git log` lists commits from newest to oldest, starting at `HEAD`. The default output is verbose; these forms are more useful day to day:

- `git log --oneline`: one line per commit (short hash and summary).
- `git log --oneline --graph --all`: an ASCII graph of all branches, showing where they fork and merge.
- `git log -p path/to/file`: every change to a file, with diffs.
- `git log -n 5` or `-5`: limit the count.

Filtering is where `log` gets powerful:

- `--author="Ada"`, `--since="2 weeks ago"`, `--until=2026-01-01`.
- `--grep="invoice"` searches commit messages.
- `-S "parseDate"` (the "pickaxe") finds commits that added or removed that string, perfect for "when did this function disappear?".
- `main..feature` shows commits on `feature` that are not on `main`.

`git show <commit>` prints one commit's metadata and diff; `git show <commit>:path/file` prints a file as it was in that commit.

`git blame file` annotates each line with the commit and author that last changed it. Use it to find the commit, then read that commit's message and diff for the *why*. `git blame -w` ignores whitespace changes, and `-L 40,60` limits it to some lines.

Commits can be named many ways: a hash prefix, a branch or tag name, `HEAD~2` (two commits back along first parents), or `HEAD^2` (the second parent of a merge).
concepts.code:
git log --oneline --graph --all -15
git log --author="Ada" --since="1 month ago" --oneline
git log -S "parse_date" --oneline        # when was this added/removed?
git log --oneline main..feature          # commits only on feature
git show 3f9a2c1                         # one commit with diff
git show HEAD~2:src/app.py               # file as it was 2 commits ago
git blame -w -L 40,60 src/app.py         # who last touched lines 40-60
takeaways: --oneline --graph --all gives a quick picture of the whole repo
-S finds commits that add or remove a string; --grep searches messages
A..B = commits reachable from B but not from A
blame finds the commit; its message tells you why
pitfalls: Treating git blame as finding who to blame — the last toucher is often just a refactor; follow the history further back.

quiz.q: Which command finds the commit that removed calls to legacy_auth()?
quiz.explain: The pickaxe -S searches diffs for changes in the number of occurrences of a string; --grep only searches messages.

quiz.q: What does git log main..feature list?
options: Commits on feature that are not on main
Commits on main that are not on feature
quiz.explain: A..B means reachable from B but not from A.

concepts.name: Ignoring files with .gitignore
concepts.summary: Keep build output, dependencies, secrets and editor junk out of the repository using .gitignore patterns.
concepts.why: A clean repo has only source files; ignoring generated files avoids noise, conflicts and leaked secrets.
concepts.body:
A **`.gitignore`** file lists patterns for files Git should treat as invisible: they won't show as untracked and `git add .` will skip them. Commit the `.gitignore` itself so the whole team shares it.

Pattern rules:

- `*.log` matches any `.log` file in any directory.
- `build/` (trailing slash) matches only directories named `build`.
- `/config.local` (leading slash) matches only at the level of this `.gitignore`.
- `**/tmp` matches `tmp` at any depth; `docs/**/*.pdf` any PDF under `docs`.
- `!keep.log` re-includes something an earlier pattern excluded. You cannot re-include a file if its parent directory is ignored.
- Lines starting with `#` are comments.

`.gitignore` files can live in subdirectories and apply from there downward. For personal patterns that don't belong in the project (your editor's swap files, `.DS_Store`), use a global ignore file set by `core.excludesFile`, or `.git/info/exclude` for one repository.

The big gotcha: **ignore rules only affect untracked files**. If a file is already committed, adding it to `.gitignore` does nothing. Stop tracking it with `git rm --cached <file>` (which keeps it on disk) and commit that.

When a file is mysteriously ignored, `git check-ignore -v <path>` prints the exact file and line responsible. Templates for most languages live at github.com/github/gitignore.
concepts.code:
cat > .gitignore <<'END'
# dependencies and build output
node_modules/
dist/
*.log
# local secrets, but keep the example
.env*
!.env.example
END

git check-ignore -v dist/app.js
# .gitignore:3:dist/    dist/app.js

# Already committed .env by mistake? Stop tracking, keep the file
git rm --cached .env
git commit -m "Stop tracking .env"
takeaways: Commit .gitignore so everyone ignores the same files
Ignore rules don't apply to files already tracked: use git rm --cached
git check-ignore -v explains why a path is ignored
pitfalls: Adding a committed secret to .gitignore and assuming it's gone — it's still in history and must be rotated.

quiz.q: config.json is already committed. You add config.json to .gitignore and edit the file. What does git status show?
options: Nothing; the file is now ignored
quiz.explain: Tracked files are always tracked; ignore patterns only affect untracked files.

concepts.name: Remotes and remote-tracking branches
concepts.summary: A remote is a named URL of another copy of the repository; origin/main is your local record of its branch.
concepts.why: Collaboration in Git is exchanging commits between repositories, and remotes are how you name them.
concepts.body:
A **remote** is a short name for another repository's URL. `git clone` creates one called `origin` automatically; in a repo you created with `git init`, you add it yourself with `git remote add origin <url>`. List them with `git remote -v`.

You can have several. In open-source work it's common to have `origin` (your fork) and `upstream` (the original project).

For each branch on a remote, Git keeps a **remote-tracking branch** such as `origin/main`. This is your local, read-only bookmark of where that branch was *the last time you talked to the server*. It only moves when you run `git fetch`, `git pull` or `git push`. It is not live: if a teammate pushes, your `origin/main` won't know until you fetch.

Your local `main` is a separate branch. Normally it has an **upstream** (tracking) relationship with `origin/main`, which is what makes `git status` say "ahead by 2, behind by 1" and lets bare `git push`/`git pull` know where to go. `git branch -vv` shows each branch's upstream and ahead/behind counts.

Other useful commands:

- `git remote show origin`: details about branches on the remote.
- `git remote rename`, `git remote remove`.
- `git remote set-url origin <new-url>`: when a repository moves or you switch HTTPS to SSH.

Remotes are just configuration in `.git/config`; you can read it to see exactly what is set up.
concepts.code:
git remote add origin git@github.com:me/notes.git
git remote add upstream https://github.com/team/notes.git
git remote -v
# origin    git@github.com:me/notes.git (fetch)
# origin    git@github.com:me/notes.git (push)
# upstream  https://github.com/team/notes.git (fetch) ...

git fetch upstream           # update upstream/* bookmarks
git branch -vv
# * main 3f9a2c1 [origin/main: ahead 2, behind 1] Fix totals
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/me/notes.git
takeaways: origin is just the default name clone gives the source remote
origin/main is a local bookmark, updated only by fetch/pull/push
Upstream tracking powers ahead/behind and bare git push/pull
pitfalls: Believing origin/main reflects the server right now — run git fetch first.

quiz.q: A teammate pushed to main five minutes ago. You haven't fetched. What does your origin/main point to?
options: The state from your last fetch, pull or push
The same commit as your local main
quiz.explain: Remote-tracking branches only update when you communicate with the remote.

concepts.name: Sharing work: push and pull
concepts.summary: Send your commits with git push and bring in others' commits with git pull.
concepts.why: These two commands are the everyday loop of collaborating through a shared repository.
concepts.body:
**`git push`** uploads your local commits to a remote branch. The first time you push a new branch, set its upstream so later pushes and pulls need no arguments:

```bash
git push -u origin feature-login
```

A push is only accepted if it **fast-forwards** the remote branch: the remote's current tip must be an ancestor of what you push. If someone else pushed first, Git rejects yours with "Updates were rejected because the remote contains work that you do not have locally". The fix is to bring their work in first, then push again.

**`git pull`** does that: it fetches new commits from the upstream and integrates them into your current branch. When both sides have new commits, it must either **merge** (creating a merge commit) or **rebase** (replaying your commits on top of theirs). Recent Git refuses to guess and asks you to choose, so set `pull.rebase` once in your config. Many teams prefer `pull.rebase true` for a linear history on personal branches.

The everyday loop on a shared branch:

- `git pull` to start from the latest state.
- Edit, `git add`, `git commit`.
- `git pull` again if time has passed, resolve any conflicts.
- `git push`.

**Never** reach for `git push --force` to get past a rejection; it overwrites your teammates' commits. If you truly need to replace a branch you own (after rebasing it, say), use `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses if the remote moved since you last fetched.
concepts.code:
git push -u origin main          # first push: set upstream
# ... later
git commit -am "Update docs"
git push
# ! [rejected] main -> main (fetch first)

git pull --rebase                # bring in their commits, replay mine on top
git push                         # now a fast-forward: accepted

git config --global pull.rebase true   # make --rebase the default
takeaways: push -u once per new branch; afterwards plain git push
Pushes must fast-forward the remote; rejections mean pull first
pull = fetch + merge or rebase; set pull.rebase to choose
Prefer --force-with-lease over --force, and never on shared branches
pitfalls: Answering a rejected push with git push --force and silently deleting a colleague's commits.

quiz.q: Your push is rejected because the remote has commits you don't have. What is the right next step?
options: Delete your local branch and re-clone
git pull (merge or rebase), then push
quiz.explain: Integrate the remote's commits first so your push becomes a fast-forward.

quiz.q: What does --force-with-lease add over --force?
options: It only overwrites if the remote is still where you last saw it
It asks the server administrator for approval
It creates a backup branch on the server
quiz.explain: The lease check fails if someone pushed since your last fetch, so you don't destroy unseen work.

concepts.name: Branches
concepts.summary: A branch is a movable pointer to a commit; create, switch and delete them freely with git switch and git branch.
concepts.why: Branches let you develop features and fixes in isolation without disturbing working code.
concepts.body:
In Git a **branch** is nothing more than a tiny file holding a commit ID. When you commit on a branch, that pointer moves forward to the new commit. **`HEAD`** says which branch you are on, so Git knows which pointer to move.

Because branches are just pointers, creating one is instant and costs nothing, which is why Git workflows use them for every feature, bug fix and experiment.

The modern commands (Git 2.23+):

- `git switch -c feature-x`: create a branch at the current commit and switch to it.
- `git switch main`: switch back. Your working tree is updated to that branch's snapshot.
- `git switch -c fix origin/fix`: create a local branch from a remote one (plain `git switch fix` does this automatically if exactly one remote has it).
- `git branch`: list local branches; `-a` includes remote-tracking ones; `-vv` shows upstreams.
- `git branch -d feature-x`: delete a branch that is merged; `-D` forces deletion of an unmerged one.
- `git branch -m new-name`: rename the current branch.

The older `git checkout` does all of this too, plus restoring files, which is why `switch` and `restore` were split out; you will still see `checkout` in many guides.

Switching with uncommitted changes works if they don't clash with the target branch; otherwise Git refuses rather than losing your work. Commit or stash first.

If you check out a commit or tag directly (`git switch --detach v1.2`), you are in **detached HEAD**: HEAD points at a commit, not a branch. New commits there belong to no branch, so create one with `git switch -c` if you want to keep them.
concepts.code:
git switch -c feature/login        # create + switch
echo "form" > login.html
git add login.html && git commit -m "Add login form"
git switch main                     # login.html disappears from disk
git branch -vv
#   feature/login 7d1c0aa Add login form
# * main          3f9a2c1 [origin/main] Fix totals
git log --oneline --graph --all
git branch -d feature/login         # error: not fully merged
git branch -D feature/login         # force delete
takeaways: A branch is a pointer to a commit; HEAD names the current branch
git switch -c creates and switches; git branch -d deletes merged branches
Detached HEAD: commits made there need a branch to be kept
pitfalls: Doing work in detached HEAD and switching away — those commits become unreachable (recoverable only via reflog).

quiz.q: What actually happens on disk when you create a branch?
options: All files are copied into a new folder
A small ref pointing to the current commit is created
quiz.explain: Branch creation writes a ref containing one commit ID, which is why it is instant.

quiz.q: You commit while on branch feature. What moves?
options: The feature pointer, to the new commit
quiz.explain: The branch HEAD points to advances to the new commit; HEAD still points to the branch.

concepts.name: Merging branches
concepts.summary: Combine branches with git merge, and know when Git fast-forwards and when it creates a merge commit.
concepts.why: Merging is how finished work lands on main; knowing the two kinds keeps history readable.
concepts.body:
`git merge <branch>` brings the commits of `<branch>` into the branch you are on. There are two outcomes.

**Fast-forward**: if your current branch hasn't moved since `<branch>` was created, its commits simply sit on top of yours. Git just slides your pointer forward; no new commit is made and history stays a straight line.

**Three-way merge**: if both branches have new commits, Git finds their **merge base** (the last common ancestor), compares each side with it, and combines the changes. It records the result as a **merge commit** with two parents. Changes to different files, or different parts of the same file, combine automatically; overlapping edits become conflicts (next lesson).

You can control which you get:

- `git merge --no-ff feature` always creates a merge commit, even when a fast-forward is possible, preserving the fact that a group of commits was one feature.
- `git merge --ff-only feature` refuses unless a fast-forward is possible. Good for updating a local `main` from `origin/main` without accidental merges.
- `git merge --squash feature` stages the combined changes as one new commit you then create, without recording the branch as merged.

After merging, delete the feature branch with `git branch -d`; its commits are safe in `main`'s history. `git branch --merged` lists branches already merged into the current one, handy for cleanup.

Merge never rewrites existing commits. That makes it safe on shared branches, at the price of merge commits in the graph.
concepts.code:
git switch main
git merge feature/login            # Fast-forward (main hadn't moved)

git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature/search -m "Merge search feature"
git log --oneline --graph -5
# *   b4e7d21 Merge search feature
# |\
# | * 91aa3c0 Add search index
# * | 3f9a2c1 Fix totals
# |/
git branch --merged                # safe-to-delete branches
git branch -d feature/search
takeaways: Fast-forward just moves the pointer; three-way merge makes a two-parent commit
The merge base is the common ancestor Git diffs both sides against
--no-ff keeps feature grouping; --ff-only refuses real merges
Merging never rewrites existing commits
pitfalls: Using --squash and then deleting the branch with -d — Git doesn't consider it merged, so -d refuses; that's expected.

quiz.q: main has not moved since feature branched off. What does git merge feature (on main) do by default?
options: Creates a merge commit with two parents
quiz.explain: With no divergent commits, Git just moves the main pointer forward.

quiz.q: Which commit does Git use as the reference point in a three-way merge?
options: The merge base, the best common ancestor
The first commit in the repository
The most recent commit by date
quiz.explain: Both sides are compared against their common ancestor to work out who changed what.

concepts.name: Resolving merge conflicts
concepts.summary: When both sides change the same lines, edit the conflict markers, git add the result and conclude the merge.
concepts.why: Conflicts are routine in team work; resolving them calmly and correctly is a core skill.
concepts.body:
A **conflict** happens when both branches changed the same lines (or one edited a file the other deleted) since the merge base. Git stops mid-merge, merges everything it can, and marks the rest. `git status` lists the files under "Unmerged paths".

Inside a conflicted file you will see:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
total = round(sum(items), 2)
=======
total = sum(items).quantize(CENT)
>>>>>>> feature/decimal
```

The top part is your current branch (`HEAD`), the bottom is the incoming branch. Your job is to edit the file into what the code **should** be, which might be one side, the other, or a combination, and delete all markers. Then:

- `git add <file>` to mark it resolved.
- When all files are resolved, `git commit` (or `git merge --continue`) to create the merge commit.

Tips that make conflicts easier:

- Set `git config --global merge.conflictStyle zdiff3`. Markers then also show the **base** version (`|||||||`), so you can see what each side actually changed.
- `git checkout --ours file` or `--theirs file` takes one side wholesale for a file.
- `git mergetool` opens a configured visual tool; most editors have a built-in conflict UI.
- Run the tests before committing the merge; a textually clean merge can still be semantically broken.

If it goes wrong, `git merge --abort` returns you to the state before the merge. The same markers and commands appear during rebase, cherry-pick and stash pop, where you continue with that command's `--continue` instead.
concepts.code:
git merge feature/decimal
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in billing.py
# Automatic merge failed; fix conflicts and then commit the result.
git status --short
# UU billing.py
$EDITOR billing.py                     # remove markers, write the right code
grep -n '<<<<<<<\|>>>>>>>' billing.py  # make sure none are left
git add billing.py
python -m pytest -q                    # still works?
git merge --continue                   # creates the merge commit

# Or bail out entirely
git merge --abort
takeaways: Conflict = both sides changed the same region since the merge base
Edit to the correct result, remove markers, git add, then continue
zdiff3 conflict style shows the base version too
git merge --abort returns to the pre-merge state
pitfalls: Committing a file that still contains <<<<<<< markers.
Blindly taking --ours or --theirs without reading what the other side changed.

quiz.q: During a merge on main of feature, what is between <<<<<<< HEAD and =======?
options: The version from main, the branch you are on
quiz.explain: HEAD is the current branch; the incoming branch's version follows the ======= line.

quiz.q: How do you tell Git a conflicted file is resolved?
quiz.explain: Staging the file marks it resolved; once all are staged, conclude the merge.

concepts.name: Fetch vs pull
concepts.summary: git fetch downloads new commits without touching your branches; git pull fetches and then merges or rebases.
concepts.why: Fetching first lets you see what changed before it lands in your work.
concepts.body:
**`git fetch`** contacts a remote, downloads any commits you don't have, and updates the remote-tracking branches (`origin/main`, `origin/feature-x`...). It never changes your local branches or working tree, so it is always safe to run.

**`git pull`** is `git fetch` followed by integrating the upstream of your current branch into it, by merge or rebase depending on `pull.rebase` or the flags `--rebase` / `--no-rebase` / `--ff-only`.

Fetching separately gives you a chance to look before you leap:

```bash
git fetch
git log --oneline main..origin/main    # what's new upstream
git diff main...origin/main            # what they changed
```

Then integrate deliberately: `git merge origin/main`, `git rebase origin/main`, or `git merge --ff-only origin/main` if you have no local commits.

Some options worth knowing:

- `git fetch --all` fetches every remote.
- `git fetch --prune` (or `fetch.prune true` in config) deletes remote-tracking branches whose branch was deleted on the server, so `git branch -r` doesn't fill up with ghosts.
- `git pull --ff-only` is a safe default for a branch you never commit to directly, such as a local `main`: it updates if possible and refuses otherwise.

A good mental model: fetch updates your *knowledge* of the remote; merge or rebase changes *your* branch. `git pull` simply does both at once, which is convenient when you already know what to expect.
concepts.code:
git fetch --prune origin
git status
# Your branch is behind 'origin/main' by 3 commits, and can be fast-forwarded.
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main     # the 3 incoming commits
git merge --ff-only origin/main          # same result as git pull --ff-only

git config --global fetch.prune true
git pull --rebase                        # fetch + rebase in one step
takeaways: fetch only updates origin/* refs; it never touches your work
pull = fetch + merge/rebase into the current branch
Fetch, inspect with main..origin/main, then integrate on purpose
fetch.prune cleans up remote branches deleted on the server

quiz.q: You run git fetch and the remote had 5 new commits on main. What changed locally?
options: Your main branch now has the 5 commits
origin/main moved; your main and files are unchanged
quiz.explain: Fetch updates only remote-tracking refs and the object database.

quiz.q: Which command shows commits that are on origin/main but not yet on your main?
quiz.explain: A..B lists commits reachable from B (origin/main) but not from A (main).

concepts.name: Undoing changes: restore and reset
concepts.summary: Discard edits, unstage files and move branch pointers back with git restore and git reset.
concepts.why: Knowing exactly what each undo command touches is what makes Git feel safe instead of scary.
concepts.body:
Undo commands differ in which of the three areas (working tree, index, `HEAD`) they change.

**`git restore`** works on files:

- `git restore file`: discard unstaged edits, copying the index version back to the working tree. The edits are gone for good.
- `git restore --staged file`: unstage, copying `HEAD`'s version into the index; your edits stay on disk.
- `git restore --source=HEAD~3 file`: bring back an older version of a file.

**`git reset <commit>`** moves the current **branch pointer** to another commit, and then optionally updates the other areas:

- `--soft`: move the branch only. The undone commits' changes stay staged. Useful to squash the last few commits into one.
- `--mixed` (default): also reset the index. Changes stay in the working tree, unstaged.
- `--hard`: also reset the working tree. Uncommitted changes are **destroyed**.

So `git reset --soft HEAD~1` "uncommits" the last commit but keeps its work staged, and `git reset --hard origin/main` throws away everything local to match the remote.

Reset rewrites the branch's history: the commits after the new position are no longer on the branch (they're still recoverable through the reflog for a while). That's fine for commits only you have, but if they've been pushed, others still have them and your next push would need force. For shared history, use `git revert`, covered next.

Before any `--hard`, run `git status` and `git stash` anything you might want.
concepts.code:
git restore config.yml               # throw away unstaged edits
git restore --staged secrets.txt     # unstage, keep the file as is
git restore --source=v1.4 -- api.py  # old version of one file

git reset --soft HEAD~3              # undo 3 commits, keep changes staged
git commit -m "Add search (squashed)"

git reset HEAD~1                     # --mixed: uncommit + unstage, keep edits
git reset --hard origin/main         # discard ALL local commits and edits
takeaways: restore = files; reset = move the branch pointer
--soft keeps changes staged, --mixed unstaged, --hard deletes them
Reset only commits you haven't shared; use revert for pushed ones
pitfalls: Running git reset --hard with uncommitted work you wanted — uncommitted changes are not in the reflog and can't be recovered.

quiz.q: You want to undo your last (unpushed) commit but keep its changes staged to recommit them. Which command?
quiz.explain: --soft moves only the branch pointer, leaving index and working tree as they were.

quiz.q: What does git restore --staged app.py do to your edits in app.py?
options: Keeps them on disk but removes them from the index
quiz.explain: --staged resets the index entry from HEAD; the working tree is untouched.

concepts.name: Reverting commits safely
concepts.summary: git revert creates a new commit that undoes an earlier one, without rewriting shared history.
concepts.why: It's the correct way to back out a bad change that others have already pulled.
concepts.body:
**`git revert <commit>`** computes the inverse of a commit's changes and records it as a **new commit**, by default with a message like `Revert "Add caching layer"`. The original commit stays in history; the branch simply moves forward.

Because nothing is rewritten, revert is safe on `main` and any branch others use. Compare with `git reset`, which moves the branch backwards and forces everyone else to deal with commits disappearing.

Useful forms:

- `git revert HEAD`: undo the most recent commit.
- `git revert a1b2c3d e4f5a6b`: several commits, each reverted in its own new commit.
- `git revert --no-commit A..B` (or `-n`): apply the inverse of a range to the working tree and index, then commit once.

If later commits changed the same lines, the revert can **conflict**; resolve it like any other conflict, then `git revert --continue` (or `--abort`).

Reverting a **merge commit** needs `-m 1` to say which parent is the mainline you want to keep, usually parent 1 (the branch you merged into). Beware a subtle consequence: Git now considers the feature's commits merged *and* undone, so merging that branch again later won't re-apply them. To bring the feature back, revert the revert.

In practice, revert is how teams roll back a deployment-breaking change quickly: revert, push, deploy, and fix forward later in a calm follow-up commit.
concepts.code:
git log --oneline -4
# e9f0b12 Add caching layer     <- broke production
# 3f9a2c1 Fix totals
git revert e9f0b12 --no-edit
# [main 5c7d8e9] Revert "Add caching layer"
git push                          # normal push, no force needed

# Undo a merge, keeping the mainline (parent 1)
git revert -m 1 b4e7d21

# Bring the feature back later
git revert 5c7d8e9
takeaways: Revert adds a new inverse commit; history is not rewritten
Safe for pushed/shared branches, unlike reset
Merge commits need -m 1 to choose the mainline parent
pitfalls: Re-merging a feature branch after reverting its merge and expecting the changes back — revert the revert instead.

quiz.q: A bad commit is already on the shared main branch. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: Delete the commit on the hosting site
git revert the commit and push
quiz.explain: Revert adds a new commit, so collaborators' history stays valid.

concepts.name: Stashing work in progress
concepts.summary: Save uncommitted changes aside with git stash, switch context, and reapply them later.
concepts.why: Interruptions happen; stash lets you switch branches without committing half-done work.
concepts.body:
**`git stash`** takes your uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged edits to tracked files), saves them on a stack, and resets your working tree to `HEAD`. You get a clean tree to switch branches, pull or test something, then bring the changes back.

Commands:

- `git stash push -m "wip: search"`: stash with a description (plain `git stash` works too).
- `git stash -u`: also stash **untracked** files, which are left behind by default.
- `git stash list`: shows `stash@{0}`, `stash@{1}`... newest first.
- `git stash show -p stash@{1}`: see what's in one.
- `git stash pop`: apply the newest stash and drop it if it applied cleanly.
- `git stash apply stash@{1}`: apply without dropping, so you can apply it elsewhere too.
- `git stash drop stash@{1}` / `git stash clear`: delete.
- `git stash branch new-branch`: create a branch at the commit you stashed from and apply it there, which avoids conflicts when the original branch has moved on.

A stash can be applied on any branch, which makes it a quick way to move uncommitted edits you started on the wrong branch. Applying can conflict; if `pop` conflicts, the stash is **kept**, so after resolving you drop it yourself.

Stashes are easy to forget, and an old stash is hard to understand. For anything longer than a quick interruption, prefer a WIP commit on a branch, or a second worktree.
concepts.code:
# Mid-feature, an urgent bug report arrives
git stash push -u -m "wip: search filters"
git switch main && git switch -c hotfix/login
# ... fix, commit, push ...
git switch feature/search
git stash list
# stash@{0}: On feature/search: wip: search filters
git stash pop                   # changes are back, stash dropped

# Started on the wrong branch? Move edits over
git stash && git switch correct-branch && git stash pop
takeaways: stash saves tracked changes and cleans the tree; -u includes untracked files
pop = apply + drop; apply keeps the stash
A conflicting pop keeps the stash so nothing is lost
pitfalls: Forgetting -u, switching branches, and finding new untracked files have followed you.

quiz.q: You ran git stash with a brand-new, never-added file in the folder. Where is that file afterwards?
options: Still in the working tree, untouched
quiz.explain: Untracked files are only stashed with -u (or -a for ignored files too).

concepts.name: Rebasing a branch
concepts.summary: git rebase replays your commits on top of another branch, giving a linear history; never rebase shared commits.
concepts.why: Rebase keeps feature branches current and history clean, but misused it rewrites others' work.
concepts.body:
Suppose you branched `feature` from `main`, made three commits, and `main` has moved on. Merging would add a merge commit. **`git rebase main`** (run on `feature`) instead takes your three commits, sets them aside, moves `feature` to the tip of `main`, and **replays** each commit on top, one by one.

The result looks as if you had started your work from today's `main`: a straight line, no merge commit, and a later merge into `main` becomes a fast-forward.

The catch: replayed commits are **new commits** with new IDs, because their parent changed. The old ones are abandoned. Hence the **golden rule: don't rebase commits that others have based work on.** Rebasing your own unpublished, or personal pushed, branch is fine; you'll then need `git push --force-with-lease` to update the remote copy.

Conflicts are resolved per replayed commit:

- Fix the files, `git add` them, then `git rebase --continue`.
- `git rebase --skip` drops the current commit; `git rebase --abort` returns everything to how it was before you started.

Merge or rebase? Both are valid; teams pick a convention. Merge preserves exactly what happened; rebase produces a history that is easier to read and bisect. A common combination is rebasing your feature branch onto `main` to stay current, and merging it into `main` via a pull request.

`git pull --rebase` is the same idea for your local commits versus newly fetched upstream ones.
concepts.code:
git switch feature/search
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
# Successfully rebased and updated refs/heads/feature/search.

# On conflict:
#   edit files, then
git add search.py
git rebase --continue      # or --skip / --abort

git log --oneline --graph -5          # linear on top of origin/main
git push --force-with-lease           # branch was pushed before: update it
takeaways: Rebase replays your commits on a new base, producing new commit IDs
Golden rule: don't rebase commits others have built on
Resolve per commit: git add, then git rebase --continue
After rebasing a pushed branch, use --force-with-lease
pitfalls: Rebasing main (or any shared branch) onto something else and force-pushing — everyone else's history breaks.

quiz.q: Why do commits get new IDs after a rebase?
options: Their parent commit changed, and the parent is part of the hash
quiz.explain: A commit's ID covers its parent; a new base means new commits.

quiz.q: Mid-rebase you realize it's a mess. What gets you back to the exact pre-rebase state?
quiz.explain: --abort restores the branch to where it was before the rebase started.

concepts.name: Pull request workflow
concepts.summary: Push a feature branch, open a pull request, get review and CI, then merge using your team's strategy.
concepts.why: Pull (merge) requests are how almost every team reviews and lands code.
concepts.body:
A **pull request** (PR; GitLab calls it a merge request) is a hosting-platform feature, not a Git command: a request to merge one branch into another, with a page for discussion, review and automated checks. Under the hood it is still branches and commits.

The typical loop:

- Update `main`, then `git switch -c feature/x`.
- Make focused commits; push with `git push -u origin feature/x`.
- Open the PR (web UI, or `gh pr create` with the GitHub CLI). Describe *what* and *why*, how to test it, and link the issue.
- CI runs tests on the branch; reviewers comment.
- Address feedback with new commits and push again; the PR updates automatically.
- If `main` moved and conflicts appear, merge or rebase `origin/main` into your branch and push.
- Merge, then delete the branch, locally and on the remote.

Platforms offer three merge buttons, and teams usually pick one:

- **Merge commit**: keeps every commit plus a merge commit.
- **Squash and merge**: the whole PR becomes one commit on `main`. Clean history; individual commits are lost.
- **Rebase and merge**: replays the commits onto `main` linearly.

For open-source contributions you usually can't push to the project, so you **fork** it, push branches to your fork (`origin`) and open PRs against the original (`upstream`).

Keep PRs small. A 200-line PR gets a careful review in minutes; a 2,000-line one gets "LGTM".
concepts.code:
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git switch -c feature/rate-limit
# ... commits ...
git push -u origin feature/rate-limit
gh pr create --title "Add rate limiting" --body "Limits /api to 100 req/min. Closes #42."

# Reviewer asked for changes
git commit -am "Address review: make limit configurable"
git push                                   # PR updates

# After merge on the platform
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git branch -d feature/rate-limit
git push origin --delete feature/rate-limit  # if not auto-deleted
takeaways: A PR is a platform feature around merging one branch into another
Push new commits to the same branch to update a PR
Merge, squash or rebase: pick one team convention
Fork + upstream remote for projects you can't push to
pitfalls: Piling unrelated changes into one PR — split them; reviewers and reverts both benefit.

quiz.q: A reviewer requests changes on your open PR. How do you update it?
options: Close it and open a new PR
Commit the fixes and push to the same branch
Email a patch to the reviewer
Push the fixes directly to main
quiz.explain: The PR tracks the branch, so new pushes to it appear automatically.

quiz.q: What does 'squash and merge' put on main?
options: Every commit from the PR plus a merge commit
A single commit containing all the PR's changes
quiz.explain: Squashing combines the PR's changes into one new commit on the target branch.

concepts.name: Tagging releases
concepts.summary: Mark release points with annotated tags, push them, and use git describe to name builds.
concepts.why: Tags give permanent, human-readable names to the exact commits you shipped.
concepts.body:
A **tag** is a name for a specific commit that, unlike a branch, does not move. Tags mark releases (`v2.4.0`), so you can always check out, diff against or rebuild exactly what shipped.

There are two kinds:

- **Lightweight** (`git tag v1.0`): just a ref pointing at a commit, like a branch that never moves.
- **Annotated** (`git tag -a v1.0 -m "Release 1.0"`): a full object with tagger, date and message, and optionally a GPG/SSH signature (`-s`). Use annotated tags for releases; tools like `git describe` and many release pipelines expect them.

Tags are **not pushed by default**. Push one with `git push origin v1.0`, all with `git push --tags`, or set `push.followTags true` so `git push` also sends annotated tags reachable from the commits you push.

Other commands:

- `git tag -l "v2.*"`: list matching tags.
- `git show v1.0`: the tag message and the commit.
- `git tag -a v0.9 3f9a2c1 -m "..."`: tag an older commit.
- `git tag -d v1.0` then `git push origin --delete v1.0`: delete locally and remotely.

`git describe` names any commit relative to the nearest annotated tag, for example `v2.4.0-12-g9c1e2ab` = 12 commits after v2.4.0, at commit `9c1e2ab`. Many build scripts embed this as the version string.

Treat published tags as immutable. Moving a release tag after people have fetched it leads to confusing mismatches; make a new version instead.
concepts.code:
git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "Release 2.4.0"
git push origin v2.4.0
git config --global push.followTags true   # push annotated tags with commits

git tag -l "v2.*"           # v2.3.0  v2.4.0
git describe                # v2.4.0-12-g9c1e2ab
git switch --detach v2.3.0  # look at an old release
git diff v2.3.0 v2.4.0 --stat
takeaways: Tags are fixed names for commits; branches move, tags don't
Use annotated tags (-a or -s) for releases
Tags aren't pushed by default: push them or enable push.followTags
Don't move published tags; release a new version
pitfalls: Tagging locally and forgetting to push the tag, so CI never sees the release.

quiz.q: You created tag v1.2 and ran git push. Does the remote have the tag?
options: Yes, all tags are always pushed
Yes, but only if it is lightweight
No, unless you push it explicitly or enable push.followTags
quiz.explain: Plain git push sends branches; tags need to be pushed explicitly or via followTags.

concepts.name: Interactive rebase
concepts.summary: Reorder, squash, reword, split or drop commits with git rebase -i before sharing them.
concepts.why: Turning a messy series of WIP commits into a clean, reviewable story is what interactive rebase is for.
concepts.body:
`git rebase -i <base>` opens your editor with a **todo list** of every commit after `<base>`, oldest first. Each line starts with a command; you edit the list, save, and Git replays the commits accordingly:

- `pick`: keep the commit as is.
- `reword`: keep it but edit the message.
- `edit`: stop after applying it so you can amend it or split it into several commits.
- `squash`: meld into the previous commit and combine the messages.
- `fixup`: meld into the previous commit and discard this message (`fixup -C` keeps this one's message instead).
- `drop` (or delete the line): remove the commit.
- `exec <cmd>`: run a shell command, such as the tests, at that point; the rebase stops if it fails.

Reordering lines reorders commits. Typical use: `git rebase -i origin/main` to tidy everything your branch adds before opening a PR.

**Autosquash** saves editing by hand. When you notice a mistake in an earlier commit, fix it and run `git commit --fixup=<that-commit>`. Later, `git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main` (or `rebase.autoSquash true`) moves each fixup under its target, already marked.

To split a commit: mark it `edit`; when Git stops, run `git reset HEAD~`, then stage and commit pieces separately, then `git rebase --continue`.

If you stack branches (`part1` on which `part2` is built), `--update-refs` moves those intermediate branch pointers along too.

All the usual rebase rules apply: new commit IDs, so only rewrite commits not yet shared, and `git rebase --abort` gets you out at any point.
concepts.code:
git commit --fixup=3f9a2c1          # "fixup! Add search index"
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main
# Editor shows (oldest first):
#   pick   3f9a2c1 Add search index
#   fixup  a77b1e0 fixup! Add search index
#   pick   5d2e9f1 WIP
#   pick   8c4b0aa Add search UI
# Change to:
#   pick   3f9a2c1 Add search index
#   fixup  a77b1e0 fixup! Add search index
#   squash 5d2e9f1 WIP
#   reword 8c4b0aa Add search UI
#   exec   make test
git push --force-with-lease
takeaways: The todo list is oldest-first; reorder lines to reorder commits
squash merges messages; fixup discards the fixup's message
commit --fixup + rebase --autosquash automates cleanup
exec runs tests at any point in the replay
pitfalls: Interactive-rebasing commits already merged into a shared branch, creating duplicate commits for everyone.

quiz.q: What is the difference between squash and fixup in the todo list?
options: squash combines messages; fixup keeps only the earlier commit's message
fixup deletes the changes; squash keeps them
squash works only on the first commit
quiz.explain: Both meld changes into the previous commit; fixup throws away its own message.

quiz.q: In which order does git rebase -i list commits?
options: Oldest first, in the order they will be replayed
quiz.explain: The todo list is a replay script, so it starts from the oldest commit after the base.

concepts.name: Cherry-picking commits
concepts.summary: Apply the changes of specific commits onto your current branch with git cherry-pick.
concepts.why: Backporting a fix to a release branch, or rescuing one commit from an abandoned branch, is a cherry-pick.
concepts.body:
**`git cherry-pick <commit>`** takes the diff a commit introduced and applies it as a **new commit** on your current branch, with the same message and author. The original stays where it was; the copy gets a new ID.

The classic use is **backporting**: a bug was fixed on `main`, and you need the same fix on `release/2.3`. You switch to the release branch and cherry-pick the fix commit.

Variants:

- `git cherry-pick A B C`: several commits, applied in order.
- `git cherry-pick A..B`: a range, excluding `A` itself (use `A^..B` to include it).
- `-x` appends "(cherry picked from commit ...)" to the message. Use it for backports so the link is traceable.
- `-n` / `--no-commit` applies changes without committing, so you can combine several picks into one commit.
- `-m 1` picks a merge commit relative to its first parent.

Conflicts are handled like in rebase: fix, `git add`, `git cherry-pick --continue`; or `--skip` / `--abort`.

Use it sparingly. Cherry-picked copies are separate commits, so if both branches are later merged, Git sees the same change twice. Usually it merges cleanly, but it can produce confusing conflicts, and `git log` shows the change twice. Prefer merging the fix branch into both places when your workflow allows it; cherry-pick is for the cases where merging would bring in too much.

`git log --cherry-pick --oneline A...B` hides commits whose changes appear on both sides, useful for spotting what was already backported.
concepts.code:
git switch release/2.3
git cherry-pick -x 7e1f3c2
# [release/2.3 4a9b0d1] Fix null check in parser
#  (cherry picked from commit 7e1f3c2...)

git cherry-pick main~5..main~2     # 3 commits: main~4, main~3, main~2
# CONFLICT in parser.py
git add parser.py
git cherry-pick --continue

# What on main is not yet on release (ignoring equivalent picks)?
git log --oneline --cherry-pick --right-only release/2.3...main
takeaways: cherry-pick copies a commit's change as a new commit on the current branch
A..B excludes A; use A^..B to include it
Use -x for backports so the origin is recorded
pitfalls: Using cherry-pick as the normal way to move work between long-lived branches — duplicate commits make later merges confusing.

quiz.q: What does git cherry-pick X..Y apply?
options: Commits after X up to and including Y
Commits from X up to but not including Y
quiz.explain: Range syntax excludes the left endpoint, so X itself is not picked.

concepts.name: Reflog and recovering lost work
concepts.summary: The reflog records every position HEAD and your branches have had, so you can undo resets, bad rebases and deleted branches.
concepts.why: It turns 'I destroyed my work' into a two-minute fix, which makes you braver with history rewriting.
concepts.body:
Every time `HEAD` or a branch moves (commit, reset, rebase, checkout, merge, amend, pull), Git appends an entry to the **reflog**. It's local only, never pushed, and it is your undo history.

`git reflog` shows `HEAD`'s log, newest first:

```text
9d2c4e1 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
5b7a0f3 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add export button
...
```

`HEAD@{1}` means "where HEAD was one move ago". `git reflog show feature` shows a branch's own log, and time-based forms such as `main@{yesterday}` work too.

Recovery recipes:

- **Undo a bad reset or rebase**: find the entry from before it, then `git reset --hard HEAD@{4}` (or the hash). After a rebase, `ORIG_HEAD` also points at the pre-rebase tip.
- **Restore a deleted branch**: find its last commit in the reflog (`git branch -D` prints the hash too) and `git branch feature <hash>`.
- **Rescue commits made in detached HEAD**: they are in `HEAD`'s reflog; create a branch at them.

Commits removed from all branches are **unreachable** but not deleted immediately. Reflog entries expire after 90 days by default (30 days for entries no longer reachable), and `git gc` then removes the objects. If even the reflog is gone, `git fsck --lost-found` can find dangling commits.

The limit: the reflog tracks **commits**. Changes you never committed or stashed, then wiped with `reset --hard` or `restore`, are not in it. Commit often and you can always get back.
concepts.code:
git reset --hard HEAD~3          # oops, those commits mattered
git reflog -5
# 9d2c4e1 HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~3
# 5b7a0f3 HEAD@{1}: commit: Add export button
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}        # back to before the reset

git branch -D experiment         # Deleted branch experiment (was 41c8e2a).
git branch experiment 41c8e2a    # restored

git rebase origin/main           # went wrong?
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD       # tip before the rebase
takeaways: Every HEAD/branch movement is logged locally in the reflog
Recover with git reset --hard HEAD@{n} or git branch name <hash>
Unreachable commits survive about 30-90 days before gc
Uncommitted work is not in the reflog
pitfalls: Expecting the reflog to exist on a fresh clone — it's local to each repository.

quiz.q: You hard-reset away three commits an hour ago. Can you get them back?
options: Yes, find them in git reflog and reset or branch to them
quiz.explain: The commits still exist as objects and the reflog recorded where HEAD was.

quiz.q: Which of these can the reflog NOT recover?
options: A branch deleted with git branch -D
Commits lost in a bad rebase
Edits never committed or stashed, discarded with git restore
quiz.explain: The reflog records commits HEAD pointed to; uncommitted edits never became commits.

concepts.name: Finding bugs with git bisect
concepts.summary: Binary-search history with git bisect to find the exact commit that introduced a bug, manually or with a script.
concepts.why: It finds the culprit among thousands of commits in a dozen steps, often fully automatically.
concepts.body:
When something worked in `v2.3.0` and is broken now, the bug was introduced by one commit in between. **`git bisect`** binary-searches that range: it checks out the midpoint, you say whether it's good or bad, and it halves the range each time. 1,000 commits take about 10 steps.

The manual flow:

```bash
git bisect start
git bisect bad              # current commit is broken
git bisect good v2.3.0      # this one was fine
```

Git checks out a commit in the middle. Test it, then answer `git bisect good` or `git bisect bad`. Repeat until Git prints "<hash> is the first bad commit". `git bisect reset` returns you to where you started.

If a commit can't be tested (it doesn't build, for example), `git bisect skip` picks a nearby one instead.

The real power is **`git bisect run <script>`**: Git runs the script at each step and reads its exit code. `0` means good, `125` means skip, any other code from 1 to 127 means bad. A failing test case makes a perfect script, and the whole hunt runs unattended.

Bisect works best when every commit builds and passes tests on its own, one more reason for small, self-contained commits. For merge-heavy histories, `git bisect start --first-parent` follows only the mainline, so it identifies which *merged PR* caused the issue.

The terms don't have to be good and bad: `git bisect start --term-old=slow --term-new=fast` finds when something *improved*.
concepts.code:
cat > /tmp/check.sh <<'END'
#!/bin/sh
make -s build || exit 125          # can't build: skip this commit
./bin/app --selftest-date-parsing  # exits non-zero when the bug is present
END
chmod +x /tmp/check.sh

git bisect start HEAD v2.3.0       # bad, then good
git bisect run /tmp/check.sh
# 7e1f3c2 is the first bad commit
# Author: ... Date: ...  "Switch date parser to strptime"
git bisect log > bisect.txt        # keep a record
git bisect reset
takeaways: Bisect halves the suspect range each step: ~log2(n) tests
git bisect run automates it: exit 0 good, 125 skip, 1-127 bad
Always finish with git bisect reset
pitfalls: Writing a run script that exits non-zero for unrelated reasons (like a build failure), so bisect blames the wrong commit — exit 125 to skip.

quiz.q: In git bisect run, what should the script exit with when a commit can't be tested?
quiz.explain: 125 tells bisect to skip the commit; 0 means good and other codes up to 127 mean bad.

quiz.q: About how many test steps does bisect need for 1,000 candidate commits?
quiz.explain: Each step halves the range: log2(1000) is about 10.

concepts.name: Multiple working trees
concepts.summary: Check out several branches at once in separate folders that share one repository with git worktree.
concepts.why: Review a PR or hotfix production without stashing or disturbing the branch you're in the middle of.
concepts.body:
Normally a repository has one working tree, so switching branches means stashing or committing your current state, and long builds or a running dev server get disrupted. **`git worktree`** lets one repository have several working trees, each with its own branch checked out, in different directories.

```bash
git worktree add ../app-hotfix -b hotfix/login origin/main
```

That creates folder `../app-hotfix`, a new branch `hotfix/login` from `origin/main`, and checks it out there. Commits made in either folder go into the same repository, so they are immediately visible from the other; no pushing or fetching between them.

Management commands:

- `git worktree list`: all worktrees, their paths and branches.
- `git worktree remove ../app-hotfix`: delete the folder and its metadata (refuses if it has uncommitted changes, unless `--force`).
- `git worktree prune`: clean up metadata for folders you deleted by hand.
- `git worktree add --detach ../tmp v2.3.0`: a throwaway checkout of a tag.

Rules and gotchas:

- A branch can be checked out in **only one** worktree at a time; Git refuses a second, to stop two folders from fighting over the same branch pointer.
- Worktrees share objects, refs, config and stashes, so they are far cheaper than a second clone.
- Each worktree has its own index and `HEAD`, and untracked or ignored files such as `node_modules` are per folder, so you may need to reinstall dependencies.

Worktrees are also a natural fit for running several tools or agents on different branches in parallel.
concepts.code:
# In ~/src/app, mid-feature with a dev server running
git fetch origin
git worktree add ../app-hotfix -b hotfix/login origin/main
cd ../app-hotfix
# ... fix, commit, push ...
git push -u origin hotfix/login
cd ../app
git worktree list
# /home/me/src/app         5d2e9f1 [feature/search]
# /home/me/src/app-hotfix  c81a7d3 [hotfix/login]
git worktree remove ../app-hotfix
takeaways: One repository, many checked-out folders, shared objects and refs
A branch can be checked out in only one worktree at a time
Remove with git worktree remove, not just rm -rf (or prune afterwards)
pitfalls: Expecting ignored files like node_modules or .env to exist in the new worktree — each folder has its own.

quiz.q: You try git worktree add ../x main while main is checked out in your current folder. What happens?
options: Both folders share main and stay in sync
Git refuses because main is already checked out
main is copied to a new branch main-2
The current folder switches to detached HEAD
quiz.explain: A branch can only be checked out in one worktree at a time.

concepts.name: Submodules
concepts.summary: Embed another repository at a pinned commit with git submodule, and keep it updated correctly.
concepts.why: Vendoring shared libraries or firmware SDKs often uses submodules, and they confuse people who don't know the model.
concepts.body:
A **submodule** is a Git repository nested inside another at a fixed path. The parent repository doesn't store the submodule's files; it stores a special entry (a "gitlink", file mode `160000`) recording **one exact commit** of the child, plus the URL in a `.gitmodules` file.

Adding one:

```bash
git submodule add https://github.com/acme/sdk.git vendor/sdk
git commit -m "Add sdk submodule"
```

Cloning a repository with submodules needs an extra step, or the folders stay empty:

- `git clone --recurse-submodules <url>`, or after a plain clone:
- `git submodule update --init --recursive`.

The key mental model: the parent **pins** a commit. Inside `vendor/sdk`, the submodule is usually in detached HEAD at that pinned commit. To upgrade:

```bash
cd vendor/sdk && git fetch && git switch --detach v1.5.0
cd ../.. && git add vendor/sdk && git commit -m "Bump sdk to v1.5.0"
```

`git submodule update --remote` does the fetch and checkout for you, following the branch configured in `.gitmodules`.

When teammates pull a commit that moved the pin, their submodule doesn't follow automatically; they run `git submodule update`, or set `submodule.recurse true` so pull, switch and friends do it.

Common traps: committing in the submodule but forgetting to push it (others then can't fetch the pinned commit), and forgetting to commit the new pin in the parent. `git status` and `git diff --submodule` show when a pin changed. If you don't need a pinned, separately versioned repository, a package manager dependency is usually simpler.
concepts.code:
git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:acme/firmware.git
cd firmware
git submodule status
#  4c1d2e3 vendor/sdk (v1.4.0)

git config --global submodule.recurse true   # pull/switch update submodules

git submodule update --remote vendor/sdk     # move to tip of tracked branch
git diff --submodule
# Submodule vendor/sdk 4c1d2e3..9a0b7f1: ...
git add vendor/sdk
git commit -m "Bump sdk"
takeaways: The parent stores a pinned commit (gitlink) plus the URL in .gitmodules
Clone with --recurse-submodules or run submodule update --init --recursive
Bumping = change the checkout inside, then commit the new pin in the parent
Push the submodule commit before pushing the parent
pitfalls: Committing a new pin to a submodule commit that was never pushed — everyone else's update fails.

quiz.q: What does the parent repository record about a submodule?
options: A full copy of the submodule's files
Only the URL; it always uses the latest commit
The URL and one exact commit ID
A zip of the submodule's history
quiz.explain: The gitlink entry pins a commit; .gitmodules holds the URL.

concepts.name: Git hooks
concepts.summary: Run scripts automatically at points like pre-commit, commit-msg and pre-push to enforce checks locally.
concepts.why: Hooks catch lint errors, bad messages and failing tests before they leave your machine.
concepts.body:
**Hooks** are executable scripts Git runs at certain events. They live in `.git/hooks/` (which ships `.sample` files to copy) or in a directory set with `core.hooksPath`. A hook is any executable named after the event, in any language with a shebang line.

Common client-side hooks:

- `pre-commit`: before the commit message is asked for. Exit non-zero to abort, which is ideal for linters and formatters.
- `prepare-commit-msg` / `commit-msg`: edit or validate the message, for example to enforce Conventional Commits or an issue ID. `commit-msg` receives the message file path as `$1`.
- `pre-push`: before anything is sent; run the faster test suite here.
- `post-checkout` / `post-merge`: after switching or pulling, for example to reinstall dependencies when a lockfile changed.

Servers have their own hooks (`pre-receive`, `update`, `post-receive`), which hosting platforms expose as protected branches, required checks and webhooks.

Two facts shape how hooks are used in teams:

- **Hooks are not cloned.** `.git/hooks` isn't versioned, so to share them commit a folder such as `.githooks/` and have everyone run `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`, or use a manager like pre-commit, Husky or Lefthook that installs them.
- **Hooks are bypassable.** `git commit --no-verify` (`-n`) skips `pre-commit` and `commit-msg`; `git push --no-verify` skips `pre-push`. So hooks are a convenience for fast feedback, and CI remains the real gate.

Keep hooks fast, a couple of seconds at most, and check only staged files, or people will start using `--no-verify` by habit.
concepts.code:
mkdir -p .githooks
cat > .githooks/commit-msg <<'END'
#!/bin/sh
# Require "ABC-123: summary" style messages
if ! head -1 "$1" | grep -qE '^[A-Z]+-[0-9]+: .+'; then
  echo "commit-msg: start the message with a ticket ID, e.g. 'ABC-12: Fix login'" >&2
  exit 1
fi
END
chmod +x .githooks/commit-msg
git config core.hooksPath .githooks
git add .githooks && git commit -m "ABC-7: Add commit-msg hook"
git commit -m "oops"        # rejected by the hook
takeaways: A hook is an executable named after the event in .git/hooks or core.hooksPath
Non-zero exit from pre-commit, commit-msg or pre-push aborts the action
Hooks aren't cloned; share via core.hooksPath or a hook manager
--no-verify bypasses them, so CI must still enforce rules
pitfalls: Forgetting chmod +x on the hook file — Git silently ignores non-executable hooks.

quiz.q: Why can't you rely on client-side hooks to enforce a policy?
options: Developers can skip them with --no-verify and they aren't cloned
Git deletes them after each commit
They run after the commit is pushed
quiz.explain: Hooks are local and optional; server-side checks or CI must enforce policy.

quiz.q: Where does a commit-msg hook find the message it should check?
options: In a file whose path is passed as the first argument
quiz.explain: Git writes the message to a file and passes its path as $1.

concepts.name: Branching strategies
concepts.summary: Compare trunk-based development, GitHub flow and Git flow, and choose one that fits how you release.
concepts.why: A shared branching convention decides how painful merges, releases and hotfixes are for the whole team.
concepts.body:
Git doesn't impose a workflow; teams agree on one. The main families:

**Trunk-based development**: everyone integrates into `main` (the trunk) at least daily, via very short-lived branches or directly. Unfinished features hide behind **feature flags** rather than living on long branches. It needs good automated tests and CI, and it minimizes merge pain because nothing diverges for long. It is the norm for teams practising continuous delivery.

**GitHub flow**: `main` is always deployable; every change is a branch plus pull request; after review and green CI it merges and deploys. Essentially trunk-based with PRs. A good default for web services and most teams.

**Git flow**: long-lived `develop` and `main` branches, plus `feature/*`, `release/*` and `hotfix/*` branches with prescribed merges between them. It suits software that ships numbered versions on a schedule and must support several in parallel, but it adds ceremony and long-lived divergence. Its own author has noted it is overkill for continuously delivered web apps.

**Release branches** combine with any of these: cut `release/2.4` from `main` at release time, stabilise and patch it (cherry-picking fixes from `main`), and tag versions on it.

How to choose:

- Deploy continuously? Trunk-based or GitHub flow.
- Maintain multiple shipped versions (mobile apps, libraries, on-prem)? Add release branches, or Git flow.
- Whatever you choose, keep branches short-lived, protect `main` (required reviews and checks), and pick one PR merge style.

The strongest predictor of merge pain is branch lifetime, not the strategy's name.
takeaways: Trunk-based: integrate daily, hide unfinished work behind feature flags
GitHub flow: main always deployable, branch + PR + deploy
Git flow and release branches suit versioned, multi-version products
Short-lived branches matter more than the strategy's name
pitfalls: Adopting Git flow for a continuously deployed web app and living with permanent develop/main drift.

quiz.q: A team deploys a web service many times a day. Which approach usually fits best?
options: Git flow with develop and release branches
Trunk-based or GitHub flow with feature flags
quiz.explain: Continuous delivery favours short-lived branches merged into an always-deployable main.

quiz.q: What lets trunk-based teams merge unfinished features safely?
options: Feature flags that keep the code inactive
Keeping the feature on a branch for months
quiz.explain: The code ships dark and is enabled when ready, so the branch never needs to live long.
